lines.pk1: Data sent over a long distance is broken into data packets, sometimes called datagrams.
lines.pk2: Each packet has three parts: a header, the payload, and a trailer.
lines.pk3: The header holds the I P address of the sender, the I P address of the receiver, the sequence number, and the packet size.
lines.ps1: In packet switching, each packet travels independently, and routers decide its route.
lines.ps2: A router picks the shortest available path, avoiding routes that are broken or busy.
lines.ps3: Packets can arrive out of order, so the receiver puts them back together using the sequence numbers.
lines.ps4: The benefit is that there are alternative routes if one is broken or overloaded. The drawback is that the data must be reassembled.
lines.outro: Split into packets, routed independently, and reassembled at the destination.
